skyline.text: How a helper sent up the road took the Vuelta
Ajay Shah’s case for know­ing a sport with­out play­ing it
Why a whole dop­ing era was struck from the record

masthead.footnote: *I have no novel insights in this episode. Page 2

brief.head: Legs, not engines
brief.text: Unlike Formula One, road cy­cling pits one body against an­other on near-identical bikes, Amit Varma said. By a Grand Tour’s third week, it be­comes “a test of pure char­ac­ter”. {053-C02}

brief.head: Orders from the car
brief.text: From the team car, a di­recteur sportif watch­ing a TV feed ra­dios in­struc­tions to the rid­ers. Strategy is de­cided be­fore a race, Amit Varma said; tac­tics dur­ing it. {053-C11}

brief.head: An hour, well lost
brief.text: Riders shar­ing a road may be play­ing dif­fer­ent games. A sprinter after the green jersey’s points will hap­pily lose an hour on a moun­tain stage, Amit Varma said. {053-C06}

brief.head: Small gains, big Sky
brief.text: Dave Brailsford’s Team Sky won seven Tours in eight years by chas­ing 1 per cent gains in diet, train­ing, po­si­tion and hel­mets, Amit Varma said. {053-C12}

brief.head: Luck of the wheel
brief.text: One touched wheel can bring down a whole group, Amit Varma said. Teams keep their lead­ers near the front of the pelo­ton, but luck re­mains huge. {053-C14}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: You don’t have to be a hen to know about eggs.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, assuring Amit Varma that a fan who cannot ride may still understand cycling

lead.kicker: Amit Varma makes the case for cycling to Ajay Shah
lead.head: Chess in the slipstream

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 53

play.label: Hear six lessons of the road

body: Amit Varma fol­lows only three sports closely. One is chess. Cricket, he told Ajay Shah, is not one of the oth­ers. Another is cy­cling, and Shah wanted to know what there was in it.

A great deal, Varma ar­gued. The sport de­mands much of the human body, spirit and char­ac­ter, and it “con­tains an el­e­ment of chess”: months of prepa­ra­tion, and deep strate­gic and tac­ti­cal thought.
He claimed no nov­elty. Nothing he would say, he warned, was un­known to peo­ple who fol­low cy­cling. He wanted to share a pas­sion, with the episode timed for the start of the Tour de France.

Nor does he ride. His thought-to-action ratio for cy­cling, he told Shah, is zero: he never learned how. “Which I used to be very em­bar­rassed about,” Varma said, “but now I’m like what­ever.” {053-S02}
## How the sport sorts it­self
Riders are sorted first by body weight, which they con­trol only so far. Light rid­ers climb bet­ter, and climb­ing, Varma said, is non-negotiable for any­one who wants to win a Grand Tour. {053-C04}

Heavier puncheurs bring ex­plo­sive power to cob­bles and short, steep hills. Sprinters save ev­ery­thing for the final stretch. Those who excel at none of these often be­come do­mes­tiques, work­ing for the team’s stars.
What makes it a team sport is physics. A rider cuts through the air and leaves a pocket of low pres­sure be­hind him; the rider tucked into it saves about 30 per cent of his ef­fort.
“All the peo­ple that you see on the screen who are cy­cling are not putting in equal ef­fort,” Varma said. {053-C03}
Almost every tac­tic fol­lows from that: do­mes­tiques shield­ing lead­ers, break­aways shar­ing turns in the wind, sprint­ers hid­ing until the last mo­ment.
## A game of lim­ited bul­lets
Early in a race, a few rid­ers break clear of the main bunch, the pelo­ton. Strangers share the work in si­lence, be­cause a lone rider can­not stay away.
Near the fin­ish, the co­op­er­a­tion col­lapses. All else being equal, the rider in front loses the sprint, so the lead­ers slow al­most to a stand­still, eye­ing one an­other.

And every rider has only so many hard ef­forts in him. When one at­tacks, the oth­ers wait for some­one else to chase. “Whoever spends en­ergy chas­ing the first guy down will not have the en­ergy to win in the end,” Varma said. “You have lim­ited bul­lets.” {053-C09}
So two team­mates can take turns at­tack­ing a lone rival until he is empty, and weaker rid­ers can wear down a favourite with­out a word ex­changed.
## Clean, and full of sto­ries
The dop­ing of the late 1990s and 2000s still shad­ows the sport. Varma ar­gued that it is by and large clean today, be­cause test­ing caught up and teams now po­lice their own rid­ers.
What keeps him watch­ing is peo­ple. “We care about key ri­val­ries, we care about re­demp­tion tales, and those mat­ter a great deal,” he said. {053-C15}
Primož Roglič, the skier turned cy­clist, still chas­ing the Tour. Tadej Pogačar against Jonas Vingegaard. Remco Evenepoel and Wout van Aert, two Belgians who some­times share a na­tional team.

Shah claimed child­hood glory rid­ing up a slope with both hands off. Had he been European, Varma sug­gested, cy­cling might have had him. “This is why eco­nomic de­vel­op­ment mat­ters,” Shah replied.
Varma closed with a dis­claimer: he is not an ex­pert, just a pas­sion­ate fan. His ad­vice was sim­pler. “Go out and watch some cy­cling right now.”

second.label: Office cricket
second.head: Dravid retires hurt
second.deck: Amit Varma’s entire cricketing record: one wide, two wickets, one thrown bat

pic.caption: Rahul Dravid in New Delhi in 2024

body: When Amit Varma was man­ag­ing ed­i­tor at Cricinfo, Rahul Dravid vis­ited the of­fice. The staff played a kind of of­fice cricket with a ball half­way be­tween a squeezy ball and a plas­tic ball. Spun for­wards or back­wards, it would zip through the air.
Varma per­suaded Dravid to bat while he bowled. His first ball was a wide. Dravid was clean bowled by the next two. {053-S01}

Dravid called him Shoaib Akhtar, re­fused to play on and threw the bat away. That, Varma said, is the sum of his ac­tion in cricket. “You would not ac­tu­ally see me on a cricket field run­ning around and doing things,” he said. “I’m Bengali.” {#bengali}

quote.text: My first ball was a wide. Didn’t work out. He was clean bowled off the next two balls.

third.head: Beaten by another planet

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Roglič’s lost Tour

body: In the Covid year, 2020, Primož Roglič led the Tour de France into its sec­ond-last stage, a time trial. His 21-year-old com­pa­triot Tadej Pogačar sat about 30 sec­onds be­hind.
Starting last, Roglič heard on the radio that Pogačar had caught his time, then passed it. On the final climb, Amit Varma said, you could al­most see tears in his eyes. {053-S12}
People called it a col­lapse. Varma calls that nar­ra­tive false. “Roglič came fifth in the stage out of hun­dred and fifty peo­ple,” he said. {#fifth} Pogačar was sim­ply on an­other planet.
Afterwards the 30-year-old Roglič found Pogačar, shook his hand and hugged him. Varma, watch­ing live, had tweeted that it was one of the sem­i­nal mo­ments in world sport.

box.title: Homework for the Tour
box.text: Amit Varma’s view­ing guide: Chris Horner, the old­est man to win a Grand Tour, who re­views each day’s rac­ing and calls waste­ful teams “knuck­le­heads”; and the *Lanterne Rouge Cycling Podcast*, whose Patrick and Benji do hour-long deep dives. {053-R04}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: No bike, no problem
sections.caption: watching a sport he cannot ride
body: Ajay Shah opened with a jab: Amit Varma, he said, looked like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle. The Bengali in Varma did not ap­pre­ci­ate the low blow. {053-J01}

Shah then rated his co-host’s “thought to ac­tion ratio” in each of his sports. Poker is high: Varma played pro­fes­sion­ally for a few years. In chess, Shah said, he has had the heart-stopping mo­ments at the board.
Cycling is zero. Varma never learned to ride. His fa­ther was in the IAS and there was al­ways a car, and his work­ing life in Bombay ran on local trains and buses until he bought one. {053-S02}
He is now, he claimed, the best driver in Bombay, “be­cause driv­ing in Bombay is not about driv­ing, it is about Bombay”. {053-J02}
## Hens and eggs

So ev­ery­thing Varma knows about cy­cling is purely in­tel­lec­tual, built from watch­ing a lot of it. Shah sup­plied the li­cence. “You don’t have to be a hen to know about eggs,” he said. “In fact, being a hen is an im­ped­i­ment to know­ing about eggs.” {053-C01}
Then he chris­tened the hour: “Welcome to a scram­bled eggs episode on cy­cling.” {053-J03}
~ It was, Shah noted at the start, an­other of the pair’s off-beat episodes, after those on chess, hik­ing and Bruce Springsteen.

quote.text: And in cy­cles, it is lit­er­ally zero be­cause I don’t know how to ride a cycle.

art.caption: Amit Varma on watching a sport he cannot ride

sections.label: The races
sections.head: Monuments, tours and a clock
sections.caption: the kinds of races
body: Amit Varma started from the ba­sics, and with road cy­cling only, not the in­door events of the Olympics.

The sim­plest race runs a sin­gle day from one point to an­other, five to seven hours in the sad­dle. Many pres­ti­gious races of this kind are called clas­sics, and five of them are the mon­u­ments: Milan-San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the Giro di Lombardia. {#monuments}

Their ter­rain dif­fers. Liège and Lombardia are hilly. Flanders and Roubaix are flat but cob­bled, which de­mands ex­plo­sive power. Milan-San Remo is flat until hills near the end, and any­body can win it.
## Against the clock
A time trial is one man against the clock. {#clock} Riders set off a minute or two apart, and one who catches an­other may not ride in his slip­stream.
Then there are the stage races: about seven im­por­tant one-week races, and three Grand Tours, in Italy, France and Spain, of three weeks each. {#grandtours}
These mix flat, hilly and moun­tain stages. A sum­mit fin­ish such as Alpe d’Huez, Varma said, sorts out the climbers. {053-J13}

~ Winning a Grand Tour, above all the Tour de France, is the great prize. Varma dis­cov­ered cy­cling watch­ing the Tour in the late 1990s, be­fore he un­der­stood its tac­tics, and saw at once the scale of the en­durance.

quote.text: That re­ally sep­a­rates the great climbers from the not so great climbers.

sections.label: The riders
sections.head: You are what you weigh
sections.caption: who climbs and who sprints
body: Cycling mixes na­ture and nur­ture, Amit Varma said, but it is a lot about na­ture, above all body weight, which a rider can con­trol only up to a point.

On long moun­tains a heav­ier rider must spend more watts to cover the same ground. So today’s Grand Tour stars, Pogačar, Vingegaard, Roglič and Evenepoel, are all light, be­tween about 61 and 65 kilos. {053-C04}
The heav­i­est top rid­ers are in the late 70s: Wout van Aert is 78 kg, Mathieu van der Poel 75. {#weights}
They are puncheurs, spelt the French way: too heavy for long climbs but ex­plo­sive on flats, cob­bles and short, steep hills, which suits them to the one-day clas­sics. {#puncheurs}
## Many races on one road
Sprinters do noth­ing all stage, shel­tered by their teams, and save ev­ery­thing for a burst over the last 30 to 70 me­tres.
Grand Tours hand out sev­eral prizes: over­all time, the Tour’s yel­low jer­sey; points, its green; and moun­tain points. {#yellow}
Riders who excel at none of these often be­come do­mes­tiques, a French term for those whose job is to help the team’s stars. {#domestique}
~ Weight is not quite ev­ery­thing. The world time trial cham­pion, Remco Evenepoel, is a GC rider of 61 kg, Varma said, and “just fan­tas­tic”.

quote.text: If you are a lighter rider, you are likely to be a bet­ter climber.

sections.label: The physics
sections.head: Thirty per cent off
sections.caption: why cycling is a team sport
body: Ajay Shah could see the pieces but not how they fit to­gether. How, he asked, does cy­cling be­come a team sport?
Through physics, Amit Varma said, in­vok­ing his co-host’s stand­ing as a card-carrying physi­cist and aero­nau­ti­cal en­gi­neer. {053-J04}
A cycle cut­ting through the air leaves a pocket of low pres­sure be­hind it, al­most a vac­uum. A rider in that pocket es­capes the wind. “I can save 30% of my ef­fort,” Varma said. {#thirty}
## Seven Amits and an Ajay
He made it con­crete. Imagine Shah as the star sprinter on a flat stage, with seven Amits on the team to pro­tect him. {#amits}
Each Amit rides in front, tak­ing the wind, until he is spent. Then he drifts aside to fin­ish at his own pace, and the next Amit takes over, until Shah is de­liv­ered to the end.

Nobody im­pro­vises alone. Every team is miked up, and a di­recteur sportif fol­lows in a car with the tele­vi­sion feed. The terms are French be­cause the French were the pi­o­neers of European cy­cling. {#french}
~ Shah had read that bas­ket­ball coaches watch their players’ live data and pull tired ones out. {#basketball} Cycling has the data, Varma said, but no rider can be swapped mid-race.

quote.text: It is the guys who are out on the wind who are putting in that ef­fort, and the peo­ple be­hind them are not.

sections.label: The tactics
sections.head: Cooperate now, betray later
sections.caption: the game theory of the breakaway
body: Strangers in a break­away share the work with­out a word, each tak­ing a turn in the wind. Sitting in with­out work­ing, Amit Varma said, is “des­per­ately un­cool”, un­less your team leader is chas­ing be­hind. {053-C08}
The pelo­ton has an edge. A break­away rider must ra­tion him­self for 100 kilo­me­tres; a do­mes­tique at the front of the bunch is told to empty him­self over 20. {053-C07}
So the chas­ing teams hold the gap at about three min­utes and time the catch for the clos­ing kilo­me­tres. Catch it too early, and an­other break­away forms.
## The Sky Train

A strong team can smother a whole race. US Postal under Lance Armstrong, and later Team Sky for Chris Froome, set a pace on the flat that no one could at­tack from, then sent moun­tain do­mes­tiques to the front one by one. {053-C10}
The pelo­ton stretched into a sin­gle line. Rivals lost their helpers; the leader kept his.
Food is tac­tics too. A rider who runs out of calo­ries has “bonked”, so the team car re­minds rid­ers to eat and do­mes­tiques ferry bars and drinks for­ward. {#bonk}
~ Are there pacts be­tween teams be­fore a race? None, Varma told Ajay Shah. Within a team, ev­ery­one knows his role, but the role is dy­namic.

quote.text: Beyond a cer­tain pace, no one can jump away from you. The ac­cel­er­a­tion and power re­quired is too much.

sections.label: The dark age
sections.head: The decade that didn’t count
sections.caption: doping and the clean-up
body: Ajay Shah raised the dop­ing ques­tion. In the Olympics, he said, it seems like an arms race where test­ing is al­ways try­ing to keep up. {#armsrace}

Cycling had one too, Amit Varma said. He re­called that Greg LeMond, or per­haps an­other top rider, took a few months off around the late 1980s and came back to find he could barely keep up with the pelo­ton. {053-S13}
Through the 1990s ev­ery­one was on drugs, Varma said, with EPO giv­ing ef­fects like those of al­ti­tude train­ing. From 1996, the Tour’s win­ners for a decade or more were all dop­ing. {#tainted}

Which is why, Varma said, it is shady to sin­gle out one vil­lain. The au­thor­i­ties did not pro­mote the run­ners-up; they de­clared that a whole period’s re­sults, all seven of Lance Armstrong’s wins in­cluded, do not count.
## Watch in good faith
The arms race ran to the start of the 2010s. Then test­ing caught up with the cheats, and teams, which suf­fer when a rider is caught, began polic­ing their own. {053-C13}
Today’s speeds, Varma ar­gued, come from bet­ter train­ing, such as weeks at al­ti­tude. Fans can watch in good faith.
~ Wout van Aert skipped this year’s cy­clocross world cham­pi­onship to pre­pare at al­ti­tude for the cob­bled clas­sics, then crashed at the Tour of Flanders through no fault of his own. {053-S14}

quote.text: They could barely keep up with the pelo­ton be­cause the pace was so in­cred­i­bly high and they re­al­ized some­thing is fishy.
We fol­low sport not just to see the lim­its of human achieve­ment, but we get caught up in the sto­ries of the peo­ple who are in­volved.

p3.title: Stories from the road
p3.deck: Decoys, stalemates and accidents: the races Amit Varma retells, and what they teach

stories.kicker: How Jumbo-Visma’s plan for the Vuelta worked too well
stories.head: The domestique who kept the jersey
body: Jumbo-Visma, then the strong­est team, came to the 2023 Vuelta a España with two lead­ers. Primož Roglič had won that year’s Giro d’Italia and the pre­vi­ous three Vueltas. Jonas Vingegaard had just won the Tour de France.
They also had Sepp Kuss, in Amit Varma’s telling one of the world’s best moun­tain do­mes­tiques, a sup­port rider who had helped Roglič win the Giro and Vingegaard the Tour.

The rival was Remco Evenepoel of Quick-Step, and the plan was clever. Send Kuss up the road in a break­away and into the leader’s red jer­sey, so that Evenepoel’s team would wear it­self out chas­ing a helper. When Evenepoel was spent, Roglič or Vingegaard would at­tack.

The plan worked too well. Evenepoel sim­ply col­lapsed, lost a few min­utes and was out of the race. Kuss led, with Roglič sec­ond and Vingegaard third. The team had the top three places, and some­one had to win.

Roglič, am­bi­tious and long un­lucky at the Tour de France, wanted to race for it. He had come there to win, he said, and should be al­lowed to beat his team­mate. Then came out­rage on so­cial media: for years Kuss had helped them win, and here was a chance, Varma said, to “gift him some­thing beau­ti­ful”. {053-S06}
Vingegaard, hav­ing just won the Tour, was cool with that. So Jumbo-Visma let Kuss win, and its rid­ers fin­ished one, two, three. {#podium}
~ Roglič was fu­ri­ous. He left for an­other team, Bora-Hansgrohe, Varma said, want­ing al­ways to be his team’s leader when he races.
stories.why: Team roles are fixed in the­ory but dy­namic in prac­tice. When a plan suc­ceeds be­yond its de­sign, loy­alty, am­bi­tion and pub­lic feel­ing col­lide, and the re­sult can cost a team its leader.
stories.postscript: Lance Armstrong once told his do­mes­tique Floyd Landis to “run like you stole some­thing”. When ri­vals held Landis, Armstrong won the stage him­self. {053-S07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Sepp Kuss’s Vuelta

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the 2022 Tour of Flanders
stories.head: Cat, mouse and three chasers
body: At the 2022 Tour of Flanders, Tadej Pogačar, 65 kg and a su­perb climber, at­tacked on the hills. Only Mathieu van der Poel, 75 kg, a lesser climber but a far bet­ter sprinter, could stay with him, Amit Varma said.

On the flat run-in, Pogačar knew he could only beat Van der Poel by com­ing out of his slip­stream. {#pogslip} So he re­fused to lead. Both slowed al­most to a stand­still, eye­ing each other, while three rid­ers be­hind, with noth­ing to lose, co­op­er­ated flat out to catch them.
They did. Van der Poel won the sprint, Dylan van Baarle was sec­ond and Valentin Madouas third. Pogačar, the dom­i­nant rider all day, was fourth.
~ That, Varma said, was “be­cause he waited too long and the other guys caught up and then he’s the worst sprinter of the bunch”. {053-S04}
stories.why: Cat-and-mouse games have a hid­den cost. While two ri­vals op­ti­mise against each other, rid­ers no­body is watch­ing can close the gap, and the clever­est move of the day be­comes self-defeating.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Pogačar’s stalemate at Flanders

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Tour de France won by being ignored
stories.head: Overlooked, then crowned
body: Contenders in a Grand Tour often let a harm­less break­away go, Amit Varma said, sure that they can catch any­one who mat­ters. The one time he re­calls it back­fir­ing was a Tour de France of 2005 or 2004; he for­got which year. The break­away car­ried Oscar Pereiro, not a great climber and not seen as a con­tender.

He gained enough time to lead the race for a while, and no­body much cared. The real fight was be­hind him, against the even­tual win­ner, Floyd Landis, if Varma re­mem­bered rightly. “All the other con­tenders were fight­ing with Floyd, so they com­pletely ig­nored this guy,” Varma said. Pereiro fin­ished sec­ond. {053-S03}
Then Landis was dis­qual­i­fied for drug use, and Pereiro be­came Tour de France cham­pion.
~ He was, Varma said, one of two lucky ben­e­fi­cia­ries; the other won last year’s Vuelta. {#lucky}
stories.why: Letting a harm­less rider go is a cal­cu­lated risk. When every rival watches one threat, the man no­body is watch­ing can walk off with the prize, and luck can fin­ish the job.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Oscar Pereiro’s lucky Tour

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Primož Roglič’s second sporting life
stories.head: From the piste to the peloton
body: Around 2007 or 2008, at a ju­nior world cham­pi­onship, a teenager from Slovenia had a ter­ri­ble ski­ing crash. Amit Varma still goes back to the footage once in a while. You worry, he said, whether he will walk again.
He was Primož Roglič. He did ski again, but re­alised he would not be among the world’s best, per­haps be­cause the in­jury cost him a de­vel­op­men­tal phase, per­haps for men­tal rea­sons.
“I love sport, man. I just love sport,” Varma re­called him say­ing. “I want to go out there, I want to com­pete, I want to be phys­i­cal.” So he took up cy­cling. {053-S11}

~ He came to it rel­a­tively late, which is why some say he is not a great bike han­dler. He be­came one of the great rid­ers of his gen­er­a­tion any­way, and won the Vuelta a España three times. {#threevueltas}
stories.why: A forced change of course, made late, can still lead to great­ness when the drive be­hind it is in­tact. Roglič’s re­demp­tion story, Varma said, has still not fully played out.
stories.postscript: In the weeks be­fore this year’s Tour, he crashed along­side Vingegaard and Evenepoel at the Tour of the Basque Country.

quiz.q: How much effort, by Amit Varma’s account, does a rider save in another’s slipstream?
quiz.a: About 30 per cent, since the rider in front takes all the wind.

quiz.q: Why did Tadej Pogačar, the day’s strongest rider, finish only fourth at the 2022 Tour of Flanders?
quiz.a: He stalled to stay in Van der Poel’s slip­stream, and three chasers caught up.

quiz.q: What did Dave Brailsford call his method of finding 1 per cent improvements everywhere?
quiz.a: The ag­gre­ga­tion of mar­ginal gains, which took Team Sky to seven Tour wins.

quiz.q: Who became Tour de France champion after Floyd Landis was disqualified for drug use?
quiz.a: Oscar Pereiro, a break­away rider the other con­tenders had com­pletely ig­nored.

quiz.q: What did Lance Armstrong tell his domestique Floyd Landis near the top of the final mountain?
quiz.a: “Run like you stole some­thing”, be­cause he wanted Landis to win the stage.

quiz.q: What is Amit Varma’s “thought to action ratio” in cycling, and why?
quiz.a: Literally zero, be­cause he has never learned how to ride a cycle.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 53. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Lance Armstrong (Josh Hallett, CC BY-SA 2.0); Rahul Dravid (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); Wout van Aert (Clémence LN, CC BY-SA 4.0); Mathieu van der Poel (Clémence LN, CC BY-SA 4.0); Chris Froome (Christophe Badoux, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.why: A first-hand ac­count of how the old­est Grand Tour win­ner pulled it off.

shelf.title: The Lanterne Rouge Cycling Podcast
shelf.creator: Patrick and Benji
shelf.why: Hour-long deep dives after races and great pre­views from two young, deeply in­volved en­thu­si­asts.

shelf.title: The ULTIMATE Tour de France 2024 Preview
shelf.creator: Lanterne Rouge Cycling Podcast
shelf.why: A ready-made primer be­fore watch­ing the 2024 Tour, which started the week­end this episode was re­leased.

shelf.title: Eurosport cycling coverage (with Dan Lloyd, Orla Chennaoui and Adam Blythe)
shelf.why: Amit rec­om­mends Eurosport be­cause the com­men­tary, es­pe­cially from Dan Lloyd, Orla Chennaoui and Adam Blythe, was one of his great joys of watch­ing cy­cling.

shelf.title: ExpressVPN (or any good VPN)
shelf.why: It is the prac­ti­cal way he has found to ac­cess cov­er­age.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Chess (Episode 52)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A syn­the­sis of Amit’s knowl­edge of and en­thu­si­asm for chess, walk­ing through every world cham­pion up to Ding and the role of com­put­ers in the game.

shelf.title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Episode 19)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s con­trar­ian ideas on cricket strat­egy and tac­tics, first de­vel­oped in 2008 and still not well un­der­stood, which he says hold truly novel in­sights.

shelf.title: Poker and Life (Episode 38)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: The Hiking Episode (Episode 35)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on his pas­sion for hik­ing, from the Goecha La trek be­neath Kanchenjunga to why the worst ac­ci­dents hap­pen when you think you’re al­most home.

shelf.title: What Bruce Springsteen Means to Us
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A labour of love about the mu­si­cian who mat­ters to both hosts, which Amit calls the show’s least-watched episode.

laughs.text: Ajay’s open­ing jab: ‘Amit, tell me, you look like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle.’ Amit: ‘This is re­ally a low blow. And the Bengali in me does not ap­pre­ci­ate this low blow.’
Amit on learn­ing to drive late: ‘I am now the best driver in Bombay. Because driv­ing in Bombay is not about driv­ing, it is about Bombay. But that is a sub­ject for an­other episode.’
Right after the hen-and-eggs line about know­ing a sport with­out play­ing it, the episode is chris­tened: ‘Welcome to a scram­bled eggs episode on cy­cling.’
Amit ex­plain­ing a break­away: ‘In a sense, when it comes to main­stream eco­nom­ics, you are a break­away, and the pelo­ton is far, far, far be­hind you.’
Amit’s VPN ad­vi­sory: ‘Young men watch­ing this for porn, okay? Do not do that. It is sin­ful, save your en­ergy for study­ing eco­nom­ics and physics and aero­nau­ti­cal en­gi­neer­ing.’
Chris Horner’s favourite ver­dict on bad team tac­tics, which Amit rel­ishes: ‘Knuckleheads.’

Cycling’s vo­cab­u­lary is largely French be­cause the French were pi­o­neers of European cy­cling: do­mes­tique, di­recteur sportif, puncheur, and rouleurs (who ‘just roll through these flat stages’).
Alpe d’Huez, the iconic Tour de France moun­tain­top fin­ish that ‘re­ally sep­a­rates the great climbers from the not so great climbers.’

Dave Brailsford, ar­chi­tect of Team Sky’s suc­cess, is now Jim Ratcliffe’s right-hand man at Ineos, which has just bought Manchester United. Manchester United is Amit’s other pas­sion, and he be­lieves Brailsford will turn it around.
